newsitem.title: GERMANY: Julius Baer sees German DAX at 3,200 in 97.
newsitem.headline: Julius Baer sees German DAX at 3,200 in 97.

text.p: Germany's blue chip DAX index, fresh from galloping past a number of record highs in recent weeks, has room to climb another 12 percent to the 3,200 level next year, Bank Julius Baer forecast on Monday.
"It is a very ambitious goal, but I think the German bourse can reach the 3,200 level next year," said Gerhard Grebe, director for research at Bank Julius Baer (Deutschland) AG.
On Monday the 30-share DAX index closed bourse trade up 2.34 percent at 2,857.24 points, making up more than half the ground lost in a global markets tumble Friday..

While the 3,000 level will be a key psychological level to break, Grebe said share market growth will be fuelled by a pickup in European economic growth as well as higher profits at German groups, reaping the benefits of massive restruturings.

Additionally a clearer picture about Europe's planned currency union, expected to raise competition on Europe's labour markets and thereby help keep wage rises low in coming years, should help boost share-market growth.

Grebe sees the currency union launched on time with the mark block, Finland and Ireland participating from the beginning. He also expects Germany to be able to push through a tough stability pact, ensuring lasting fiscal discipline, which would help markets.
"The cyclical environment is positive and some building blocks have been laid for rising profits," Grebe said.

Noting that German companies' willingness to embrace the concept of shareholder value has been rewarded by the markets, Grebe added, "the German market will become slightly more Americanised and that will lead to higher share-market levels."
With U.S. economic growth expected to slow next year, Grebe said Europe will take over the role as a locomotive for growth from the U.S.

In Germany, Grebe predicts gross domestic product to be 2.3 percent next year and 3.1 percent in 1998 with west German growth climbing 2.3 percent in 1997 and 3.1 percent in 1998. In east Germany growth is seen totalling two percent next year and 1.8 percent in 1998.
Growth will again be driven largely by exports, but inflation rates are seen remaining steady, which will allow the Bundesbank to keep interest rates steady for some time.
"The first interest rate hike should come up for discussion sometime in the first quarter 1998," Grebe said.
In the bond market Grebe predicts a small increase in yields, with capital market rates rising to around 6.3 percent by the end of 1997 from levels of around 5.77 percent now.

The U.S. dollar, whose stronger level benefited German exporters this year, is expected to come off a little next year as the economy slows, but Grebe said the effect should not be problematic for German companies as they now calculate for a dollar level of 1.40 marks, not 1.50 marks as was the case earlier.
Bank Julius Baer recommends shares in German bank Commerzbank AG, Daimler- Benz AG and Linde AG as well as Fresenius Medical Care AG, Sdzucker AG and Vossloh AG.
